chapter_title: Writing Your First Smart Contract in Hardhat

screens.title: Writing Your First Smart Contract in Hardhat
screens.subtitle: From project file to a working Counter contract — learn the Solidity basics and safe patterns.

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will take an empty Hardhat project and write a working Solidity contract called Counter. I’ll guide you through the essential file conventions — the SPDX license comment and the pragma directive — and show why they matter for reproducible compilation and licensing. You will see how to declare a state variable, initialize it inside a constructor, add a read-only function that returns the stored value, and add three state-changing functions: increment, decrement with a safety check, and setCount. Along the way we’ll point out common mistakes like wrong visibility, forgetting data locations for complex types, and how underflow used to be handled before Solidity 0.8.0. By the end you’ll understand how a simple contract is structured and why mutability, visibility, and require checks shape secure behavior on-chain. This orientation will make the step-by-step live-coding clear and practical, and prepare you to attempt the Wallet lab that follows. Think about what state you want your contract to own and why you’d restrict who can change it.

keyIdea.title: Start small, think about safety
keyIdea.text: A single contract shows core Solidity concepts: versioning, state, visibility, mutability, and defensive checks. Build incrementally and validate assumptions with require.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Writing Your First Contract
Writing Your First Smart Contract in Hardhat
A hands-on walk-through of Counter.sol and the Solidity building blocks you will use every day.
In this lesson
Create contracts/Counter.sol, add pragma and SPDX, declare state, write constructor and functions with safe checks, and run simple compile tests in Hardhat.
Why it matters
Correct syntax and visibility determine both safety and usability of your contract. Small mistakes cause compilation or runtime failures that cost gas and developer time.
Explore Key Topics
Pragma & Compiler
Set compatible compiler versions so your code compiles predictably.
State & Visibility
Decide what data is stored and who can access or modify it.
Safety Checks
Use require and simple guards to prevent invalid state transitions.
Concept Snapshot
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Counter Contract
A minimal contract that stores a number and exposes safe methods to read and update it. Good first project to learn Solidity basics.
Flow
Create file → Add pragma & SPDX → Define state → Initialize in constructor → Add view and transactional functions.
Getting Ready
Open your project in VS Code and create contracts/Counter.sol. We will use Hardhat's compile and test tools after writing the contract.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on practical skills you will use the moment you open V S Code. First, you will create a new Solidity file inside the Hardhat project structure so your contracts are discovered by the compiler. I’ll explain where files live and why the contracts directory matters. Second, you will write a simple contract with a state variable, constructor, and a set of functions that read and update state. This practice makes core concepts concrete — state persists on chain and functions change it. Third, we’ll cover the pragma and SPDX lines that sit at the top of every Solidity file. You will learn what each one communicates to the compiler and to users, and how the caret operator affects version compatibility. Fourth, you will apply basic Solidity syntax: choose data types, set visibility and mutability, and call require for simple checks. Each objective includes a short skill explanation and a competency milestone so you can verify your progress. By the end you'll not only have code but a mental checklist to avoid common beginner mistakes.

keyIdea.text: By following these objectives you'll produce a working contract and know the exact reasons behind each line you write.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.subtitle: Translate each objective into a small coding task you can run locally

narration.text: This page turns objectives into short, verifiable tasks you can complete in your editor. First task: create contracts/Counter. sol and confirm Hardhat compiles it. This ensures the project layout is correct and the compiler can see your file. Second task: implement _count as a state variable, add a constructor to set it, and write getCount as a view function. Run a read-only call in a script or REPL to confirm it returns the initial value. Third task: add the pragma line and SPDX identifier at the top, then run compilation to make sure there are no version mismatches. If the compiler warns, adjust the caret or Hardhat config. Fourth task: implement increment, decrement (with require), and setCount. For each function, write a tiny test or console. log script to exercise it. These hands-on checks convert knowledge into verified competency and help you spot visibility and mutability mistakes quickly. Ask yourself: can I explain why each function costs or does not cost gas?

keyIdea.title: Turn objectives into tests
keyIdea.text: Small, repeatable tasks and quick compile/tests are the fastest way to confirm you understand each objective.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Practice & Verification
Turn objectives into quick checks
Each learning objective maps to a short action: create file, compile, run a view call, write a test for a state change. Use these checks to build confidence.
Quick Checklist
  • Create contracts/Counter.sol and run npx hardhat compile.
  • Add pragma and SPDX-License-Identifier, then recompile to confirm compatibility.
  • Implement getCount as a view and call it locally to verify return value.
  • Write tests or script to call increment, decrement and setCount to assert state changes.
Verified Competency
If compilation and simple tests succeed, you can claim competency in basic contract authoring and state management.
Bloom's Focus
Apply and test. Make the contract do something and verify it behaves as expected.
Common Pitfall
Forgetting the contracts folder or naming mistakes prevents Hardhat from compiling your file. A compile failure is often a path or pragma mismatch, not always a code bug.

screens.title: Project structure & creating Counter.sol
screens.subtitle: Where to place Solidity files and why the contracts directory matters

narration.text: Before you write a single line of Solidity, place your file where tools expect it. Hardhat conventionally looks for source files under a contracts directory. Creating contracts/Counter. sol signals the build system to compile, create artifacts, and enable scripts to deploy the contract. Practically, that means when you run the compile task, Hardhat reads all files inside contracts and reports errors with file paths that match your editor. A concrete example: adding a file named Counter. sol in the root instead of contracts will lead to 'no contracts found' or simply no artifacts, which feels like a mysterious failure. Another key reason to keep a dedicated contracts folder is separation of concerns: tests, scripts, and front-end code live elsewhere, making maintenance easier. A common misconception is that any. sol file anywhere will be compiled automatically; the toolchain relies on conventions in configuration. To verify your setup, create contracts/Counter. sol, add a small contract skeleton, then run npx hardhat compile. If you see an artifact for Counter, the step succeeded. Reflect: if compilation fails, is it the file location, the pragma mismatch, or a syntax error?

keyIdea.title: Follow project conventions
keyIdea.text: Place Solidity files in contracts/ so Hardhat discovers and compiles them; this prevents confusing missing-artifact errors.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Project structure
Create contracts/Counter.sol
Put every contract file under the contracts folder so Hardhat compiles and generates artifacts predictably.
Process Steps
  1. Create a file named contracts/Counter.sol.
  2. Add top-level pragma and SPDX-License-Identifier.
  3. Write a minimal contract skeleton and run npx hardhat compile.
  4. Confirm artifact appears in artifacts/.
Common mistake
Saving the file in the wrong folder or using an unexpected file extension prevents automatic discovery and compilation.
Live-coding layout
Editor: skeleton file
// contracts/Counter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.9;

contract Counter {
  // skeleton: state and functions will be added in later steps
}
Why this matters
Conventions reduce friction: compilers, deployment scripts, and tests expect a standard layout. Staying conventional avoids time-consuming debugging of tool configuration.
Check
Run npx hardhat compile. If you see a Counter artifact, you are ready to add logic.

screens.title: Pragma & SPDX-License-Identifier
screens.subtitle: Versioning and license comments that live at the top of every Solidity file

narration.text: Two lines at the top of a Solidity file do more than look formal. The SPDX license comment communicates the code's licensing intent to humans and automated scanners. In examples we often use UNLICENSED during development, but for published code you should choose a clear license like MIT. The pragma directive declares which compiler versions the file is compatible with. For example, pragma solidity ^0.8.9 indicates any 0.8. x compiler starting at 0.8.9 and below 0.9.0 is acceptable. This caret operator avoids accidental compilation with a newer, potentially breaking compiler. A concrete example: if your pragma is too loose you might compile with a newer compiler that introduces changed behavior, or if it is too strict your CI may fail. A common misconception is that pragma is optional; without it the compiler will not know which language features or safety checks apply. To validate, change the pragma to a safe range that matches your Hardhat config and run a quick compile. The takeaway: always set an explicit pragma and add a license line to make your intent explicit and your build reproducible.

keyIdea.title: Directive and license
keyIdea.text: Pragma pins acceptable compiler versions; SPDX states license intent. Both improve reproducibility and legal clarity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Pragma & SPDX
Top-of-file directives
These two lines set compiler boundaries and license information for people and tools that inspect your source.
Example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.9;
Here the caret allows 0.8.9 up to, but not including, 0.9.0. If you need a specific patch, avoid the caret and use an exact version.
Why it matters
Compiler changes can introduce subtle behavioral differences. A clear pragma protects you from accidental breaking changes, and a license comment makes legal status explicit for downstream users.
Common misconception
Pragma is not decorative: missing or incorrect pragma leads to warnings or compilation mismatch. Never rely on default behavior.
Check
Match your pragma to the compiler version used in hardhat.config.js and run a compile to confirm there are no compatibility warnings.

screens.title: Contract structure & state variables
screens.subtitle: Define contract, state variables, and visibility — why uint256 and private matter

narration.text: The contract block is the unit of deployment and encapsulates data and behavior. When you write contract Counter {... } you declare a named container stored on chain. State variables declared at the top, like uint256 private _count, become part of the contract's persistent storage. Choosing uint256 is a common default because it offers a wide non-negative range suitable for counters. Visibility matters: private restricts access to inside the contract, preventing external reads or writes; public exposes state or creates an automatic getter. A concrete example: declaring _count as private prevents external contracts or users from reading it directly, yet you can provide a public view function to expose a controlled representation. One misconception is assuming private means encrypted on chain — it does not. The value is still visible in transaction traces and block data; private only prevents direct Solidity-level access. The practical takeaway is to choose visibility intentionally, and use public getters or view functions for any values you want readable off-chain. Contract structure & state variables means state variables persist on-chain; visibility controls solidity-level access, not blockchain secrecy.. In practical terms, define contract, state variables, and visibility — why uint256 and private matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Storage is explicit and visible
keyIdea.text: State variables persist on-chain; visibility controls Solidity-level access, not blockchain secrecy.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › State Variables
State variables and visibility
Use appropriate types and visibility to express who may read or change data.
Example declaration
uint256 private _count;
This stores a non-negative integer in contract storage. private prevents other contracts from calling a Solidity-level selector to access it, although the stored value is still part of the chain state.
Misconception
private does not encrypt or hide data on-chain. Anyone inspecting the chain can still see stored values.
Architecture Snapshot
Contract
Encapsulates state and methods. The contract name defines the on-chain object you deploy.
State Variable
Persistent storage on the blockchain; choose types and visibility for correct semantics and gas cost considerations.
Quick rule
Use uint256 for counters and be explicit about visibility. Provide controlled access through view functions rather than exposing mutable state directly.

screens.title: Constructor and initialization
screens.subtitle: How constructors run once to initialize contract state and optional deployment parameters

narration.text: A constructor is a special function executed a single time during deployment. It sets initial state and can accept deployment-time arguments. In our Counter example the constructor sets _count to zero, guaranteeing a known starting state. Constructors are executed in the deploy transaction and any state changes they make become part of the deployed contract. A common practice is to accept initial values as constructor parameters to avoid a separate initialization step. For example, you might accept an initialCount argument and assign it to _count, so deployments can vary by environment. A frequent misconception is trying to call the constructor after deployment; constructors cannot be invoked again. Another pitfall is forgetting to set the owner or essential state in the constructor, leaving the contract in an unintended default state. When writing constructors test them by deploying a fresh instance in a script or test and asserting the initial state. This ensures the contract starts where you expect and avoids manual configuration steps later. Constructor and initialization means constructors run once during deployment to set initial state. use parameters to make deployments configurable and predictable.. In practical terms, how constructors run once to initialize contract state and optional deployment parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: One-time initialization
keyIdea.text: Constructors run once during deployment to set initial state. Use parameters to make deployments configurable and predictable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Constructor
Constructor usage
Use the constructor to establish a reliable initial state at deployment time.
Example
constructor() {
  _count = 0;
}
Or accept parameters to initialize different deployments: constructor(uint256 initialCount) { _count = initialCount; }.
Test
Deploy a fresh instance in a test and assert getCount returns the expected initial value.
Misconception
Constructors are not callable after deployment. Any required setup should happen inside the constructor or through explicit functions guarded by access checks.
Why it matters
Failing to initialize important state may leave the contract unusable or insecure. Make initialization explicit and test it.

screens.title: getCount — view functions and gas-free queries
screens.subtitle: How view functions work and why they don't cost gas when called externally

narration.text: View functions let you read on-chain state without modifying it. When a function is marked view, calls that run locally from your development machine do not create a transaction and therefore do not consume gas. That makes view functions ideal for exposing read-only data such as a counter value. In our Counter contract getCount is declared public view returns (uint256). This explicitly communicates that it will not modify state and will return a numeric result. A concrete example: calling getCount from a Hardhat script using a provider will perform an eth_call and return the current _count without spending Ether. A common misconception is that view functions are free in all contexts; if a view function is called inside a transaction by another contract, it executes as part of that transaction and contributes to gas used by the overall call. Always remember view means "doesn't modify state on its own" but it can be used inside transactions. For a quick validation, deploy the contract locally, call getCount, and observe no gas cost reported for the call itself. What read-only values will your contracts need to expose?

keyIdea.title: Read-only access
keyIdea.text: View functions are for reading state. They avoid gas for external calls but can still take part in transactions when invoked from other contracts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › getCount
getCount: a view function
Returns the current counter value without modifying contract state when called off-chain.
Code
function getCount() public view returns (uint256) {
  return _count;
}
Practical check
Call getCount from a script or console and confirm the provider returns a numeric result without creating a transaction.
Context
View is a mutability tag. It communicates intent and informs callers that the function will not persist state changes when executed as an eth_call.
Gotcha
Calling a view function inside another transaction contributes to gas for that transaction. view does not magically make transactions free.
Key Takeaway
Use view for read-only operations and confirm with an eth_call during development.

screens.title: increment — state changes and gas cost
screens.subtitle: Implementing a state-modifying function and understanding transaction effects

narration.text: State-modifying functions change on-chain data and therefore require a transaction and gas. increment() in our Counter sets _count = _count + 1. When you call increment from a signer it creates a transaction, miners include it in a block, and the state is updated globally. A concrete example: send a transaction from a local test account and then call getCount to confirm the state increased by one. Remember that every storage write is the costliest operation in terms of gas, so minimize writes when possible. A common beginner error is assuming a function annotated with no mutability tag is automatically free; only view and pure are free for off-chain calls. Also avoid redundant storage updates like writing the same value back into storage unnecessarily. For testing, run two sequential transactions and assert count increases each time. Finally, consider event emission for important state changes so off-chain systems can watch and react without constantly polling the contract state. increment — state changes and gas cost means functions that write to storage consume gas and must be invoked as transactions; test these using a signer and then read the changed state.. In practical terms, implementing a state-modifying function and understanding transaction effects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transactions change state
keyIdea.text: Functions that write to storage consume gas and must be invoked as transactions; test these using a signer and then read the changed state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › increment()
Incrementing state
A simple state change demonstrates the transaction lifecycle and gas implications.
Code
function increment() public {
  _count = _count + 1; // or _count++;
}
Test tip
Call increment from a signer and then call getCount to confirm the new value. Each write costs gas; use local networks for quick iteration.
Gas note
Storage writes are expensive. Batch writes and avoid unnecessary storage churn to keep user costs low.
Pro-tip
Emit an event on important state changes so off-chain services can react without polling contract state continuously.

screens.title: decrement — require checks and underflow protection
screens.subtitle: Use require to validate state before mutation and prevent invalid underflow behavior

narration.text: Decrementing numeric state requires a guard to prevent the counter from going negative. In Solidity 0.8 and above arithmetic underflows revert automatically, but adding an explicit require statement improves clarity and provides a helpful error message. The pattern require(_count > 0, "Counter cannot go below zero"); followed by _count-- ensures the contract only executes the decrement when safe. A concrete scenario: if your contract had no guard and an underflow occurred, older compilers would wrap the value, producing a very large number and unexpected behavior. Many learners mistakenly trust automatic checks without informative messages. Using require gives readable feedback that aids debugging and user interaction. Test this by calling decrement when the count is zero and confirm the transaction reverts with the expected message. This practice formalizes correctness and makes your contract safer and easier to maintain. decrement — require checks and underflow protection means use require for logical guards and to provide explicit error messages that help callers understand why a transaction reverted.. In practical terms, use require to validate state before mutation and prevent invalid underflow behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Defensive programming
keyIdea.text: Use require for logical guards and to provide explicit error messages that help callers understand why a transaction reverted.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › decrement()
Safe decrement pattern
Validate preconditions with require to avoid invalid state transitions and provide a clear reason on revert.
Code
function decrement() public {
  require(_count > 0, "Counter cannot go below zero");
  _count--;
}
Runtime check
Call decrement when _count is zero and confirm the transaction reverts with the error message to validate your guard works.
Why explicit checks
Explicit requires provide readable errors, which improves developer and user experience when transactions fail.
Misconception
Relying solely on implicit arithmetic checks can leave you without a helpful error message. Use require to clarify the condition that failed.

screens.title: setCount — function parameters and assignments
screens.subtitle: Accepting inputs and updating state via function parameters

narration.text: Functions can accept parameters to update contract state with externally provided values. setCount(uint256 newCount) demonstrates passing an unsigned integer into a function and assigning it to storage. This shows how arguments flow from the transaction call to the contract and then into storage. A concrete use case is allowing an administrative account or a test script to reset the counter to a known value. You should validate incoming parameters when appropriate; for example, ensure newCount is within acceptable bounds. A common mistake is forgetting that function parameters for dynamic types need explicit data locations like memory or calldata — although for value types like uint256 this is not needed. Also remember visibility and access control: if setCount is public without checks, anyone could change the counter. Consider adding access control or limiting this function to tests and removing it in production. After adding setCount, write a test that passes a specific value and asserts getCount returns that value to validate the parameter passing flow. setCount — function parameters and assignments means function parameters carry external inputs into contract logic — validate and protect them to maintain correctness.. In practical terms, accepting inputs and updating state via function parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Parameter flow
keyIdea.text: Function parameters carry external inputs into contract logic — validate and protect them to maintain correctness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › setCount()
Accepting and assigning parameters
Parameters let you set state based on external input; validate when appropriate and consider access control.
Code
function setCount(uint256 newCount) public {
  _count = newCount;
}
Security note
If setCount is public, anyone can call it. Add owner checks or remove test-only setters before production deployment.
Parameter rules
Value types like uint256 do not require data location specifiers. For strings and arrays, use memory or calldata to avoid compilation errors.
Check
Write a test that calls setCount with a chosen value and asserts getCount returns that value immediately after the transaction is mined.

screens.title: Visibility, mutability & data locations
screens.subtitle: Contrast correct and incorrect uses to avoid common compilation and security errors

narration.text: Three related areas cause frequent beginner errors: visibility, mutability, and data locations. Visibility controls who can call or access functions and state. A variable declared public produces a getter; private does not. Mutability tags like view and pure declare whether a function reads or modifies state. Data locations are required for reference types such as strings and arrays; forgetting memory or calldata causes compilation errors. Consider a concrete contrast: declaring a function without visibility can result in unexpected default visibility, making it callable or not according to Solidity's rules and producing security holes. Another example is omitting memory for a string parameter passed to a public function — the compiler will raise an error telling you to add a data location. A common misconception is that the compiler will infer the right location; in practice you must be explicit. To avoid mistakes, always annotate visibility and mutability and specify memory or calldata for dynamic parameters. When in doubt, run the compiler and read the diagnostic; the error messages are precise and help you fix these common issues quickly. Visibility, mutability & data locations means always specify visibility, mutability, and data locations. compiler diagnostics guide you to correct mistakes early.. In practical terms, contrast correct and incorrect uses to avoid common compilation and security errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Be explicit in declarations
keyIdea.text: Always specify visibility, mutability, and data locations. Compiler diagnostics guide you to correct mistakes early.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Visibility & Mutability
Correct vs Incorrect
Compare right and wrong patterns to internalize best practices and compiler expectations.
Correct
function getCount() public view returns (uint256) { ... } — explicit visibility and mutability.
Incorrect
function doSomething(string s) public { ... } — missing data location for string parameter causes a compile-time error.
Checklist
  • Always include visibility: public, private, internal, or external.
  • Mark read-only functions with view or pure.
  • Specify memory or calldata for dynamic parameters like string or bytes.
Why it matters
Being explicit makes your contract's surface stable and easier to audit, and avoids frustrating compiler errors during development.

screens.title: Implement the Wallet starter: requirements & starter code
screens.subtitle: A lab: create Wallet.sol with owner, deposit, getBalance, and withdraw guarded by require

narration.text: Now apply the same patterns to a practical lab: implement a simple Wallet contract. The requirements are straightforward but reinforce key ideas. First, include pragma and SPDX at the top. Second, store an owner address as a public state variable and set it in the constructor to the account that deploys the contract. Third, implement a payable deposit function so anyone can send Ether to the contract. Fourth, implement getBalance as a public view function that returns address(this). balance. Fifth, implement withdraw allowing only the owner to withdraw a specified amount, using require to check both caller authorization and contract balance. The starter code intentionally leaves TODOs so you can practice adding constructor logic, the payable modifier, and require checks. After implementing, write a test that deploys the contract, calls deposit with some Ether, asserts getBalance reflects the deposit, and then withdraws as the owner while a non-owner withdraw attempt reverts. This exercise ties together ownership, payable functions, balance checks, and require-based validation — all central Solidity skills. Implement the Wallet starter: requirements & starter code means the wallet lab combines constructor initialization, payable deposits, balance reads, and guarded withdrawals to practice core solidity patterns.. In practical terms, a lab: create wallet.sol with owner, deposit, getbalance, and withdraw guarded by require. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab: Wallet contract
keyIdea.text: The Wallet lab combines constructor initialization, payable deposits, balance reads, and guarded withdrawals to practice core Solidity patterns.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Wallet Starter
Activity: Implement Wallet.sol
Follow the TODOs in the starter to practice constructor assignment, payable functions, and require checks for withdrawals.
Starter Code
// contracts/Wallet.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: UNLICENSED
pragma solidity ^0.8.9;

contract Wallet {
    address public owner; // State variable to store the owner's address

    constructor() {
        // TODO: Set the owner to the address that deploys this contract
    }

    // TODO: Implement a deposit function that allows sending Ether to the contract
    // Hint: Use the 'payable' modifier

    // TODO: Implement a getBalance function that returns the contract's Ether balance
    // Hint: Use 'address(this).balance'

    // TODO: Implement a withdraw function that allows only the owner to withdraw
    // Hint: Use 'require(msg.sender == owner, "Not authorized");' and 'require(address(this).balance >= amount, "Insufficient balance");'
}
Testing checklist
  • Deploy Wallet and confirm owner equals deployer.
  • Call deposit with Ether and assert getBalance increases.
  • Attempt withdraw as non-owner and expect revert.
  • Withdraw as owner and assert balance decreases appropriately.
Why this lab
It combines constructor initialization, payable functions, balance access, and require-based access control — essential building blocks for dApp logic.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts
Pragma solidity
Pins compiler compatibility to avoid unexpected behavior across versions.
SPDX-License-Identifier
